opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a useful marker because if you look at what a five-year-old can do, it's really quite remarkable, and most of it happens before any formal education begins. By that age, a child can see the world in three dimensions, recognize thousands of object categories, navigate through cluttered environments, pick up and manipulate objects with real dexterity, and understand a good deal about how the physical world behaves. Things fall, things are solid, things persist when you can't see them. They also have a working command of their native language and a surprising degree of social understanding. They can infer what other people want, what they know, what they intend.

What strikes me is that none of this is taught in a classroom. The child acquires it through interaction: moving around, touching things, playing, observing the people around them. It's embodied, multimodal, and largely self-supervised. Then school starts, and that's when we layer on the things we used to think of as the hallmarks of intelligence: reading, arithmetic, formal reasoning, chess, and so on.

And here's the irony for AI. For a long time, the field treated those later, school-type skills as the hard problems. It turns out they're comparatively easy for computers. What's hard is what the five-year-old already has. This is essentially Moravec's paradox. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years refining perception and motor control, and only a tiny sliver of time on abstract symbolic reasoning. So the five-year-old represents the foundation, the substrate on which everything else is built.

So when I think about building general intelligence, I find it a helpful target. Before we worry about machines writing essays or proving theorems, can we build something that understands and acts in the physical world the way a five-year-old does? If we can get that foundation right, I suspect a lot of the higher-level capabilities become much more grounded and robust. Without it, we risk building systems that are very fluent but don't really understand the world they're talking about.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the way to think about it is this: by the time a child is five years old, they have essentially acquired all the fundamental capabilities that make us human, and they've done it without going to school. Think about what a five-year-old can do. They can see, they can navigate the world, they can manipulate objects with their hands, they can talk and understand language, they understand something about other people's intentions. They have a fairly sophisticated intuitive physics and intuitive psychology. And all of that gets built up in those first few years, largely through interaction with the world rather than through explicit instruction.

Then from five onwards, what happens? You go to school, you learn to read, you learn arithmetic, you learn history, and so on. That's what I would call the cultural layer, the stuff that's been accumulated by civilization over thousands of years. And that's actually, in some sense, the easier part. It builds on top of this foundation that was laid in the first five years.

So for me, the reason this matters for AI and robotics is that we've kind of done it backwards. We've been quite successful at the post-five-year-old stuff, the abstract symbolic knowledge, the things that are written down in books and on the internet. Large language models are extraordinarily good at that. But the first-five-years part, the sensorimotor intelligence, the ability to perceive and act in the physical world, that's where we're still quite far behind. And it's not coincidental that it's harder. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on that part, and it's the part a child masters before any formal teaching begins. That's a very strong hint about where the real difficulty lies, and about the order in which these capabilities might need to be built.

astra-6.text:
Well, by the age of five, a child has acquired an extraordinary range of capabilities. They can see and recognize things, understand and speak language, move around in the world, and manipulate objects. They also have a working understanding of other people—what someone might want, what they might know, how they might react.

And all of this happens before much formal schooling. We tend to associate intelligence with things like mathematics or chess, but those come later. The foundation is this ability to perceive, act, communicate, and learn from everyday experience. A five-year-old still has a great deal to learn, of course, but already has a remarkably general and flexible intelligence. That makes it a very useful milestone when we think about what we want our AI systems to achieve.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, by the age of five, a child has acquired a remarkable range of abilities. They can see and understand the world, recognize objects, understand language, carry on a conversation, and act in their environment. They can walk, run, pick things up, and manipulate them. And they have some common-sense understanding of how the world works and how other people behave.

Of course, a five-year-old still has a great deal to learn. But the foundations are already there. Much of what comes later builds on those capabilities. So I think it’s a useful milestone for AI: can we build a system with that broad foundation, with perception, action, and language working together? The interesting thing is that children acquire these abilities largely through everyday experience, before years of formal education.
